To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified the salivary gland transcripts of the Hyalomma d. tick, which is the most abundant tick species in deserts of North Africa and the Middle East, and we have identified gender-specific differences in the salivary transcripts that may explain differences in blood-feeding strategies of males and females.

we have sequenced, assembled and annotated the sialotranscritomes of male and female H.dromedarii and found differences in expression of some genes that might be involved in the blood-feeding strategy of both genders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the feeding strategies of male and female H dromedari.
the discovery of new molecules of potential pharmacological interest and the elucidation of their biological activities in order to develop new strategies for controlling tick-borne diseases.
the identification of new pharmacological targets and the development of new drugs for the control of hard ticks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work provides an insight into the molecular basis of the interaction between H. dromedarirum salivary molecules and host defense systems.
H. dromadarii sialome is a valuable resource for the discovery of novel anti-coagulants and immunomodulators.
the sialome of the H. dromedaritick is a rich source of proteins that may be involved in the modulation of the host's hemostatic, inflammatory and immune response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have provided a valuable resource for future research on H. dromadarii and other tick species of the genus  Hyalomma.
we provide a valuable resource for further functional and comparative studies of H. dromoedarii sialogenome.
the H. dromadarii salivary transcriptome has a great potential to be exploited for the development of novel anti-tick drugs and vaccines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gender differences in gene transcription are reflected in the expression of salivary proteins that may play a role in the blood-feeding process.
the sialome of female H. d romedarii is more complex than that of males and that it is enriched with transcripts encoding molecules that are involved in host hemostasis and immunity.
H. dromemarii females and males employ different strategies during feeding.
